headlines.title: Motorcyclist dies in solo crash on Highway 85 in Los Gatos
headlines.description: A motorcyclist died in a collision over the weekend in Los Gatos, the California Highway Patrol said Monday. On Saturday just after 3 p.m., CHP officers responded to a collision on the northbound state Route 85 to state Route 17 transition road. According to investigators, a motorcycle driver failed to properly traverse the cloverleaf transition and instead drove off the roadway. The exact time and cause of the crash are currently under investigation, the CHP said.

headlines.title: Multi-day treasure hunt kicks off in San Francisco
headlines.description: Keep your eyes peeled, San Francisco. A multi-day treasure hunt featuring thousands of dollars in prizes kicked off Tuesday. Rare coin dealer Stack’s Bowers Galleries is hiding prize certificates at iconic locations across the city every day through Saturday. The company will post clues on its Instagram page each day at noon. If you find a certificate, you can redeem it for rare coins or other collectibles, with some prizes valued at up to $3,500.

headlines.title: Palo Alto tightens restrictions on overnight RV parking
headlines.description: Palo Alto is getting stricter with RV parking on public property, with more residential streets set to become off-limits. The city has been working to curtail RV and other large vehicle parking on city streets. New no-overnight-parking signs will go up around Palo Alto’s city limits, announcing parking restrictions on streets within 100 feet of residential areas, including areas zoned for housing and mixed-use sites. There will be no parking between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m., doubling the hours when parking is restricted. The city estimates there are about 150 RVs on city streets that people are living in.One issue the City Council will revisit is the 100-foot zone. “It’s not just an arbitrary number, but I think that there’s some considerations there in terms of how you do the actual measurement of that as well and also how it affects each neighborhood,” Councilmember Ed Lauing said. The council will return to the issue in two weeks.

headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. headlines.title: Sen. Adam Schiff raises concerns after SFO immigration holding facility visit
headlines.description: U.S. Sen. Adam Schiff toured an immigration holding facility Tuesday at San Francisco International Airport, where he says some travelers are being held longer than policy allows and without being able to communicate with family or legal counsel within a reasonable timeframe. Schiff says the same thing is happening in Southern California. The senator said the Department of Homeland Security has been using a holding area to detain immigrants for longer than the 72 hours allowed when Customs and Border Protection flags them upon returning from international travel. Schiff says some of those being detained are lawful U.S. residents who get stuck in the system. NBC Bay Area’s Kris Sanchez has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: Santa Clara Valley Water declares emergency ahead of potential winter storms
headlines.description: Santa Clara Valley Water declared a precautionary emergency in Santa Clara County to prepare for potentially severe winter storms and flooding. The declaration follows Gov. Gavin Newsom’s statewide emergency proclamation last month, which was prompted by forecasts of a strengthening El Niño pattern that could bring above-average rainfall to Northern California. The emergency allows Valley Water to quickly purchase equipment, stockpile flood supplies and secure services to protect infrastructure. Residents are encouraged to prepare emergency plans, sign up for alerts and locate free sandbag stations ahead of winter.

headlines.title: SFDA charges construction company, 3 supervisors in deadly 2023 trench collapse
headlines.description: A construction company and three project supervisors were charged in the death of an employee who was crushed when a trench collapsed in San Francisco in 2023, the district attorney’s office said Monday. Alameda County resident Javier Romero, 25, was killed after he became trapped under 8 feet of dirt when a trench collapsed in the area of Oak and Divisadero streets in San Francisco on Sept. 28, 2023. According to prosecutors, Romero was working on a sewer upgrade project in a 2.5-foot wide, 5-foot long, and 8-foot-deep trench that was not properly supported, and when a vehicle drove by, it collapsed. Romero worked for D’Arcy & Harty Construction Inc. and was part of a project for the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission, according to the district attorney’s office. Charged in his death with allegations of involuntary manslaughter and violations of safety standards are San Francisco residents John Darcy, 62, and John Tobin, 39, and Richmond resident Filiberto Poblano Perez, 52. D’Arcy & Harty Construction Inc. was also charged in connection with the death. All three defendants and the company have pleaded not guilty. Darcy was the site safety representative designated by the company and Tobin was the project manager. Poblano Perez was the crew foreman who directly supervised Romero, prosecutors said. According to the district attorney’s office, the state workplace safety inspector who reviewed the fatality concluded that the 8-foot-deep excavation in which Romero died was not properly supported. The short sides of the trench facing Oak Street on one side and facing a building on the other side were completely unsupported, prosecutors allege. The long sides of the excavation running perpendicular to Oak Street were only partially supported. D’Arcy & Harty Inc. had been the subject of a safety complaint about an inadequately supported trench on another project less than three weeks before the excavation collapse that killed Romero, according to prosecutors.
headlines.source: Katy St. Clair | Bay City News

headlines.title: Bonta advises against crypto ATMs, warns of prolific scams
headlines.description: California Attorney General Rob Bonta warned residents Monday to be on the lookout for several different types of fraud and scams related to cryptocurrency that have been reported recently. The advisory came as part of an ongoing effort by the Attorney General’s Office to keep the public informed about risks associated with cryptocurrency. Americans lost about $11.4 billion to cryptocurrency-related scams in 2025, according to the FBI’s Internet Crime Center. Bonta’s advisory came days after a settlement was announced between the Attorney General’s Office and Fidelity Digital Asset Services that resolved complaints that the company was restricting customers from withdrawing funds when they wanted to. A similar settlement was reached with Robinhood Crypto in 2024. Bonta declined to say at a press conference in San Francisco’s Potrero Hill neighborhood on Monday whether there were any other investigations into other companies engaged in similar activity. But he warned of a variety of scams and “red flags” that residents in the state should be aware of related to the crypto industry, including those that use artificial intelligence to mimic a familiar person’s appearance or voice, and so-called “meme coins” that are backed – or appear to be backed – by a celebrity or influencer. Such cryptocurrency coins are known for a type of scam called a “rug pull,” in which the issuer of the digital currency attracts investors, driving up the price, before suddenly selling a large share that lets them make a profit but drives the price down for investors, making the coins essentially a way to transfer wealth to the issuer. Recent instances of allegations of rug pull scams have been leveled against President Donald Trump, former president Joe Biden’s son, Hunter Biden, and influencer Hailey Welch, known as the Hawk Tuah Girl. Rug pull scams are also perpetrated by online groups that enthusiastically back a coin and hype it to other online users, only to sell their shares and devastate new investors. Bonta singled out cryptocurrency ATMs as one of the riskiest crypto products and said they should never be used. The machines allow users to buy, sell, and transfer cryptocurrency in-person by accessing digital “wallets” that are used as crypto accounts. They are often placed in businesses by third party companies that Bonta said skirt consumer protection laws because of the anonymous nature of cryptocurrency wallets. There are at least 60 in San Francisco, according to the state Department of Financial Protection and Innovation. Many of them are located in Safeway grocery stores. While operators are supposedly licensed by the state and therefore publicly available, visits to multiple local stores and a Google search revealed there are likely many more than the state’s list shows. In response to a question about legislation to ban the machines, Bonta said it would be up to policy makers to craft such a bill and he would not comment on hypothetical legislation. But he said while they are in operation, crypto ATMs should be universally avoided. “Never use a crypto ATM,” Bonta said. “Never use them. Don’t use crypto ATMs. Scammers push victims to these machines because, once the money goes in, it can’t be reversed, it can’t be easily traced. These ATMs are not backed by trustworthy companies and lack consumer protections.” Vermont, Tennessee, Minnesota, and Indiana have passed legislation banning the machines. In California, the city of San Diego is considering local legislation to require scam warning signs on the ATMs, which are also referred to as kiosks. Bonta said other scams to be aware of include what is known as “pig butchering,” which involves a person pretending to be a love interest who requests large sums of money from victims. “Sextortion” occurs when someone threatens to release compromising material, such as photographs or videos, in exchange for money or some other demand. Bonta advised victims of such scams to ignore threats and block anyone making them. He said the maneuver is most often a bluff, and that the material is rarely released. “Liquidity mining” is a type of scam that promises passive income by connecting a real digital wallet to a fake one, and is often deployed on gaming platforms. The scam involves displaying a fake dashboard to make the user think they are collecting small amounts of cryptocurrency over time, only to see their real assets wiped out. He said other classic scam routines such as gaining a person’s trust through phone calls and other contacts and obtaining passwords or other sensitive information have also been reported, in some instances targeting a previous scam victim by pretending to be someone who can help them recover their money from the first scam. Beware of promises of large returns for small investments, be cautious about unsolicited emails or phone calls and do not provide personal information, Bonta advised. Verify the contact with the source before providing any information by calling the purported business directly and double-checking email addresses. Pause and take nine seconds before acting. The signing of Senate Bill 1208 in early October by Gov. Gavin Newsom will help the Attorney General’s Office have new tools to recover stolen cryptocurrency, according to Bonta, who sponsored the legislation. He said the law would make it easier for investigators to access stolen funds. “It allows them to petition a court to return the cryptocurrency to victims, even when the perpetrators are outside of US jurisdiction,” he said. Bonta also urged victims not to be embarrassed, as scams have proliferated and become sophisticated and have entrapped a variety of victims. Scams involving cryptocurrency and other types of financial manipulation can be reported to the Attorney General’s Office at oag.ca.gov/report.

headlines.title: Vallejo homeowner considers legal action against PG&E after tree removal leaves massive log pile
headlines.description: A Vallejo homeowner is considering legal action against Pacific Gas and Electric Co. after utility crews removed a large tree from her backyard in June but left behind a massive pile of heavy logs. Catherine, a Vallejo resident, said she understood why the tree needed to come down because it was overgrown and leaning dangerously close to power lines. “The tree was overgrown and close to the lines so it was going sideways so it was better to remove it,” Catherine said. However, crews left behind a pile of large logs that she says she cannot move on her own, creating an obstacle and a potential safety hazard. “Well I can not walk…blocks my way around the property, and it’s close to my house…this is flammable material,” Catherine said. According to PG&E’s online policy regarding tree safety work, branches under 4 inches thick are generally chipped or removed, while larger wood is left on the property for the homeowner to manage. Even so, Catherine maintains that a PG&E inspector verbally promised that someone would return to haul the logs away or cut them into pieces so she could dispose of them herself. She could not provide written documentation of the agreement. “Those are absolutely unspeakable,” Catherine said. “That it’s left to myself, an elderly lady to handle, there’s no way I can handle it.” Describing the situation as an unfulfilled promise, Catherine expressed deep frustration. “On one hand PG&E doing a good job cleaning the trees but on the other hand they’re leaving behind huge debris for people to do what?” she asked. “This is vandalism and my property it’s intentional…elderly abuse….infliction of emotional distress,” Catherine added. PG&E officials stated that the utility is looking into the matter. In a statement, the company said: “We’re taking this seriously and are now reviewing our records to get a better understanding of what work we were doing at this customer’s address. We expect to have those details tomorrow.” Catherine said that if the issue is not resolved this week, she plans to move forward with legal action.

headlines.title: San Francisco faces deadline to submit bid to buy PG&E assets
headlines.description: Tuesday is the deadline for San Francisco to submit an official bid to state regulators if the city wants to operate its own power company. San Francisco is offering $3.4 billion to buy PG&E’s assets, but NBC Bay Area’s Investigative Unit has learned PG&E will counter with a price of at least $20 billion. In its offer, San Francisco is not including what city officials said are costs the city will bear on its own, such as creating a new station to handle getting power and delivering it to the grid. PG&E includes those larger costs. San Francisco said it has recorded 40 power outages so far this year. City leaders continue to ask state regulators to get to the bottom of what they call the utility’s reliability issues. San Francisco Apr 21 San Francisco Mar 31 PG&E disagrees. Last week, CEO Patti Poppe told the Climate One group that PG&E actually has less outage time this year. Poppe also said San Francisco is vastly underestimating the cost of taking over the utility and undervaluing its assets. “I imagine there will be a convoy of blue and white trucks driving across the Bay Bridge to Oakland, never to come back,” Poppe said. “I don’t think that’s in San Francisco’s best interest. And we’ll fight about that.” San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu said the city will likely rehire many of those workers. Chiu called Poppe’s talk of a $20 billion value “absurdly inflated,” citing the city suffering one major outage a week on average. The California Public Utilities Commission is in the process of determining a fair and just value for a potential sale. That process will take time, and the issue could also end up in court.

headlines.title: Proposal to turn abandoned SF Centre mall into data center and AI lab faces pushback from Mayor Lurie
headlines.description: The abandoned San Francisco Centre mall could find new life as a massive data center and artificial intelligence lab under a newly revealed proposal, though the idea faces immediate hurdles from city leadership and community members. The multistory shopping mall has been closed and boarded up since late January. According to a proposal confirmed by Jared Kreiger, CEO of the Maryland-based property development firm KG Growth Partners, a confidential client is exploring purchasing the entire property to convert the upper floors into a data center and AI lab. The plan would include public space on the ground level and water for a rooftop community garden that could be donated to nonprofits focusing on food insecurity. However, Kreiger declined to reveal the identity of the prospective buyer. The proposal comes at a complicated time for downtown San Francisco. Last week, Mayor Daniel Lurie approved a 45-day moratorium on City Hall approving any permits to build new data centers in the city. Addressing the proposal, Mayor Lurie said he was unaware of the plan and emphasized that the building remains on the market. “I am not aware of that proposal,” Lurie said. “The building is still up for sale. There is not a buyer yet. I’m hopeful that we get someone in there that will bring a lot of people downtown.” Communities across the country have increasingly raised concerns over data center developments, pointing to issues such as heavy water usage, environmental impacts, round-the-clock noise, and vibrations. Local reactions to the downtown San Francisco concept were mixed. “I’ve heard bad things about data centers,” said San Francisco resident Paul Bodner. “By default I would not support it,” added Guillaume Le Ster, also of San Francisco. Nicholas McNely, who lives a couple of blocks from the shuttered mall, questioned the motives behind such a project. “They’re more trying to extract from whatever community they’re trying to extract the resources from to enrich themselves so, I don’t really see the reason for a data center here,” McNely said. Conversely, some visitors saw potential upside. Janet Li of Burlingame noted, “If it’s an AI center here, more people would work here so, I think it’s good for the street.” The proposal was first reported by the San Francisco Chronicle and confirmed to NBC Bay Area by development consultants.

headlines.title: Federal grant cuts threaten South Bay housing program for 40 vulnerable patients
headlines.description: A South Bay community clinic is scrambling to secure alternative funding after federal grant cuts slashed more than $400,000 from a vital housing program, leaving 40 vulnerable patients at risk of losing their homes. Bay Area Community Health, which operates clinics from Hayward to Gilroy, recently learned that its annual funding for the Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS program has dried up. Dr. Zettie Page, president and CEO of BACH, said the clinic only found out about the cuts a week ago. Noting that the health centers primarily serve uninsured, underinsured, and special populations cycling in and out of employment, Page emphasized that stable housing is a vital pillar of health care. “Because our health centers really focus on uninsured and underinsured, and those who have neither, we really work to target those in special populations, and those who are in and out of employment,” Page said. “We just became aware of this a week ago,” Page added. “So the what now is still on the table.” The sudden funding cliff forced BACH to notify the 40 affected families that their housing subsidies will end on Oct. 30 — less than two weeks away. NBC Bay Area reporter Damian Trujillo noted that because these individuals are already in highly vulnerable situations, there are deep concerns they could end up on the streets. San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan placed the blame squarely on federal decisions, sharply criticizing the cuts. “Forty vulnerable people potentially right out on the streets,” Mahan said. “Medically vulnerable. They cannot work. They have life-altering medical conditions.” “We need to shine a spotlight on the cruelty of the Trump administration’s policies,” Mahan added. “These are health care and housing cuts that are targeting the most vulnerable people.” Mahan stated that the city cannot afford to backfill the $400,000 due to its own ongoing budget shortfalls. Instead, city leaders are actively engaging with the South Bay congressional delegation and hoping the county will release Measure A funds intended for emergencies of this scale. “I think it’s irresponsible,” Mahan said. “I think it’s cruel, and this is what these policies look like in practice.” NBC Bay Area reached out to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development for comment but has not yet received a response. Meanwhile, BACH staff remain devastated, worried that the impacted families face severe uncertainty heading into the cold winter months and the holidays.
